title: An Inflatable Pool Party by Craig & Karl Fills a Dubai Atrium with Summer Fun
description: At ICD Brookfield Place in Dubai, a vibrant collection of smiling inflatables sprouts from a vaulted ceiling, creating a suspended pool party of c
body:
At ICD Brookfield Place in Dubai, a vibrant collection of smiling inflatables sprouts from a vaulted ceiling, creating a suspended pool party of colorful forms. The spirited installation is titled “Under the Sun” and the latest project by duo Craig & Karl. 
“We wanted to capture the warmth, vibrancy, and joy of summer—distilled into one space and experienced from within the expansive summer garden atrium. A way to bring the season indoors,” the pair write about the project. Included in the installation are hot-weather staples like flowers, beach balls, inner tubes, and of course, a radiant sun.

The immersive work is a new installment in Craig & Karl’s Mateys universe, populated by a vivid array of inflatable characters. Whether springing up on a bridge or dangling from the ceiling as in Dubai, the expressive forms infuse oft-overlooked architecture with play and whimsy.
Although the duo live in different cities—Craig in New York and Karl in London—they continue to collaborate across continents, allowing projects to “unfold as a two-way conversation from the initial idea through to completion, with each of us throwing things out, building on the other’s ideas, and knowing when something feels right.” This collaboration works, in part, because the artists met while in college and spent a considerable time in the same studio, securing a bond and trust in another that’s indelible to their current practice.
Keep up with Craig & Karl and their globe-trotting projects on Instagram.

title: Estefania Ajcip's Sculptural Paintings Unite the Memories of a Separated Family
description: Through vivid sculptural paintings, Los Angeles-based artist Estefania Ajcip peers in on the fractures families face when split apart. Ajcip spent
body:
Through vivid sculptural paintings, Los Angeles-based artist Estefania Ajcip peers in on the fractures families face when split apart. Ajcip spent much of her childhood in Guatemala, while her father worked in L.A. and missed pivotal moments of her youth. In a new body of work titled Folded Memories, the artist contends with this adolescent experience, extrapolating her recollections into poignant compositions filled with a longing for connection.
From birch plywood, papier mache, small LED lights, and acrylic, Ajcip constructs a surreal world in which childhood grief and dreams converge. She often works from family photos, pulling scenes and objects from her home and pushing them into a fantastical realm. “Momo 2012,” for example, depicts two adults grasping hands, while an opening in the wood reveals a forlorn girl and her paper train set. 
“Telephone game” (2026), birch plywood sheet, foam board, thread, matte gel, acrylic on panel, 36 x 24 x 8 inches
Separations and fissures recur throughout the pieces, evoking the distance between Acjip and her father, while new details are revealed or concealed depending on the viewer’s perspective. In “Telephone game,” the artist appears with a paper phone and string held up to her ear, while her father stands at a public payphone that juts out from the two-dimensional canvas.
A similar perspective shift occurs in “Four paths/Two paths?” as a sculptural bus shuttling between L.A. and Guatemala. The latter’s national bird flutters at the vehicle’s front window, leading the way as a symbol of togetherness and hope. A statement adds that the piece most directly confronts “the familial unity that Ajcip so longed for throughout her childhood. Across the exhibition, Ajcip makes clear again and again how the longing that defined her youth now fuels her art, a powerful reminder that strength often grows in adversity.”
Folded Memories is on view through August 22 at Charlie James Gallery in Los Angeles. You also might be interested in the architectural portraits of Arghavan Khosravi.

title: On Vintage Boards, Lou Benesch Conjures the Fantastic World of The Magician
description: Enter The Magician’s Room, and you’ll encounter a brawny horse with a serpent coiled on its back, a flock of headless birds diving into a central
body:
Enter The Magician’s Room, and you’ll encounter a brawny horse with a serpent coiled on its back, a flock of headless birds diving into a central star, and a fluffy white rabbit framed by an unblinking circle of eyes. This surreal, liminal space is the setting for a new body of work by Paris-based Lou Benesch.
On view through August 22 at Hashimoto Contemporary, the solo exhibition takes the tarot’s Magician card as a starting point. Known as a trickster-wizard who connects the heavens and earth, the mysterious figure is primed for movement and change. Benesch translates the Magician’s inclination for action and mysticism into a collection of dreamy works on found and antique materials.
“The Magician’s Room” (2026)
Vintage board games and chalkboards become the aged frames for the artist’s energetic mixed-media compositions, while antique paper holds bold two-dimensional depictions of hybrid creatures and otherworldly happenings. The Magician’s Room melds past and present and spiritual and physical into a fantastic alternate word where dreams and manifestation rule.
If you’re in San Francisco, stop by Hashimoto Contemporary to see the exhibition before it closes on August 22. Otherwise, keep up with Benesch on Instagram.

title: At This Year's Rencontres d'Arles, Photography Rethinks Its Centers
description:
Features
                The art world at times imagines itself outside politics, or at least agrees on them; the latest edition
body:
Features
                The art world at times imagines itself outside politics, or at least agrees on them; the latest edition of the annual festival reveals otherwise.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Thato Toeba, "civilians I "(2025), collage, glass and wood (photo Mario Todeschini, courtesy the artist and Stevenson, Cape Town / Amsterdam; all other photos Daniela Mayer/Hyperallergic unless noted)
    
        
            ARLES, France — When the 57th Rencontres d’Arles photography festival opened in the second week of July, its 47 exhibitions filled the ancient churches, modern galleries, and unconventional venues of Arles with contemporary photographs, and almost no air conditioning. Sweaty yet jovial visitors moved through Roman and medieval structures and along bustling streets lined with Parisian-priced cafés, carrying personal Evian misters and plastic spinning fans, new staples of the European summer in the age of climate crisis. Opening week drew 22,000 people, nearly half the population of Arles, a small French city on the Rhône once home to Vincent Van Gogh, yet everyone appeared to know everyone, or at least to know who everyone was. The festival runs through October 4, with a season pass costing €42 euros.More than 115 public events took place over the first week — artist panels, curator tours, book signings at the Arles Books Fair, an open-air cinema program by the documentary platform Tënk, sponsored parties that ran into the small hours — and the majority were free. Some ancillary, unofficial, art-world gatherings required an invitation; the rest simply required knowing where they were happening. “It doesn’t have as much pretension as a lot of the other [art] events — although people who have been coming longer would probably push back on that,” said Perry Shimon, a contributing editor at Autre and curator of Filoxenia: Queer Joy in the Mediterranean, a film and photographic project showcased at the festival.Charlotte Yonga featured in The Best Possible Way to Tell the Truth… curated by Nadine HounkpatinDirector Christoph Wiesner wrote in the catalog that “as everything pushes toward simplification, division and reduction,” the 57th edition of the Rencontres d'Arles would create a space for “complexity and attentiveness.” This year, that center space is given over to those whom the Western canon long consigned to its margins — though the festival itself avoids this vocabulary.

title: A View From the Easel
description:
Community
                “A ritual I have is to always scribble a line or word, or poem that stayed with me while listening to
body:
Community
                “A ritual I have is to always scribble a line or word, or poem that stayed with me while listening to an audiobook or song, onto the wall in my studio.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Welcome to the 351st installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Rah Naqvi paints with soil and tends his studio as a garden of creativity.Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.Rah Naqvi, Amsterdam Noord, NetherlandsHow long have you been working in this space?Almost four years.Describe an average day in your studio.I have been listening to the anarchist audio library lately as I work. My routines shift greatly because I don’t believe in working solely within the studio; so much of what I am moved by comes from outside.On a studio working day, I’d have my coffee in the studio and start playing around with the work I intend to make. The audiobook usually fluctuates between a world radio station and excerpts of the book I’m listening to. I definitely work on multiple things at once because I get bored and distracted quite easily. The scattered interests keep me engaged longer, so I feel more fulfilled in the different mediums I am able to play around with. I think that really helps each medium better the other. A ritual I have is to always scribble a line or word, or poem that stayed with me while listening to an audiobook or song, onto the wall in my studio. It helps me keep track of what moved me and stays there as a reminder.

title: UT Austin’s Harry Ransom Center Provides Funded Fellowships in the Arts and Humanities
description:
Announcement
                The humanities library and museum will award up to 50 fellowships to support scholars, artists, and writ
body:
Announcement
                The humanities library and museum will award up to 50 fellowships to support scholars, artists, and writers conducting on-site archival research.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            The Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin invites applications for its 2027–2028 research fellowship program. Up to 50 fellowships will be awarded to support projects that require substantial on-site use of the center’s internationally renowned collections in the humanities.Fellowships are open to graduate students, current and former academic faculty at any career stage, and independent researchers — including journalists and artists — whose work engages deeply with archival materials. Residency lengths range from one week to two months, with stipends provided to support travel and research.The center’s collections span literature, photography, film, art, and cultural history, offering rich opportunities for interdisciplinary exploration. Recent acquisitions that are now accessible to researchers include the Lorne Michaels Collection, Ethel Waters Papers, and Irwin Winkler Papers.Research conducted by humanities scholars contributes to a dynamic body of knowledge that reshapes our understanding of what is preserved and valued in our communities. Applicants are encouraged to review the individual residency types and qualifications outlined in the application instructions. The deadline to apply is 5:00 pm, CST on November 6, 2026.About the CenterThe Harry Ransom Center is a humanities research library and museum that supports discovery, creativity, and scholarship. Its collections include nearly 45 million literary manuscripts, one million rare books, five million photographs, and more than 100,000 works of art.To learn more, visit ransom.center/fellowships.

title: Miles Greenberg Rehearses Myths for the Future
description:
Art Review
                The artist’s performance videos invoke the wild, inestimable human spirit and make Black people the c
body:
Art Review
                The artist’s performance videos invoke the wild, inestimable human spirit and make Black people the characters of universal stories.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Installation view of Miles Greenberg, "TЯUTH" (2023), 3-channel video, duration: 15 minutes, at the Current (photo courtesy the Current, all other photos Seph Rodney/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            STOWE, Vt. — Across three adjacent screens, a warrior slathered in black oil and clothed only in dark briefs draws her double-edged sword, carefully, ceremoniously, across another combatant’s. The opponent falls back, both sword arm and sword outstretched to keep her at bay. The warrior grips her blade with her naked left hand, applies force. Her opponent sinks to her knees still holding her own sword like a talisman, like a shield, like a plea for détente. The aggressor pulls back as murky crimson water swims up and around both warriors’ legs. Around them swirl six other performers, all armed with swords and clothed similarly, with their skin wholly coated in a dark lubricant so that only their palms, the insides of their ears, or their gleaming teeth break the obsidian spell. Even the typically white sclera of their eyes look dark (an effect I find out later is produced by wearing contact lenses) so they seem like members of an alien race performing a ritual of yet unknown significance.Detail of Miles Greenberg, "TЯUTH" (2023), 3-channel video, duration: 15 minutesI am watching “TЯUTH,” a three-channel video installation by Miles Greenberg at his solo show at the Current in Stowe, Vermont. The video is a lyrical, 15-minute distillation of a seven-hour durational performance staged in 2023 at Powerhouse Arts in Brooklyn, New York. Though the performers, who are all Black, make dramatic cuts and parries, as a former fencer I can tell they have carefully rehearsed, not intending to hurt each other. Greenberg confirmed this, conveying to me via the Current’s curator and executive director, Rachel Moore, that the swords are steel but the edges dulled. Regardless, the scenes are visually arresting. Throughout the video most of the engagements shown involve two fighters, but one scenario involves several fighters attempting to subdue a single warrior, which raises the stakes of danger, though I am relatively sure no one will be harmed.One of the most entrancing moments arrives when Greenberg, who is one of the performers, draws the flat of his sword against his tongue, thus transferring the black pigment to his mouth as he smiles conspiratorially at the camera. I am reminded of Friedrich Nietzsche’s contention in his  On the Genealogy of Morality that the human animal was originally incalculable and wild, not acting in predictable, normalized ways. He argues that our development of custom, law, and punishment has caused us to become calculable despite our chaotic animal nature. In an adjoining gallery, another video work even more powerfully invokes that sense of our wild, inestimable spirit.Detail of Miles Greenberg, "LE MIROIR" (2025), 6-channel video, duration: 15 minutes“LE MIROIR,” a six-channel video presentation displayed on six monitors installed in a circle, is the second and final work in this show. It consists of an edited recording of a 2025 performance at Marrakesh's historic El Badi Palace for the 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair, combined with footage shot in the Emirati desert on the border with Oman. There are 10 performers, again covered in black pigment and clothed in black athletic wear at various points in the video, standing atop plinths with mirrored surfaces and seated within a serene pool of water. The plinths are the mirrors, reflecting the surrounding landscape as the performers strike stylized and statuesque poses. Their sclera and irises here appear all white, again making them seem like users of magic, and they are attended by local animals that might represent their familiars: piebald pythons and white storks. At one point, a lone man sits atop a mirrored disc in a modified lotus position while a python swirls around his bare neck, chest, and shoulders. A significant part of the work follows Greenberg and another man engaging in physical play: walking while holding hands, tumbling down a desert dune together, carrying each other on their backs. The Current describes the work as “a surreal queer love story inspired by the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice,” which seems plausible but may be a bit too precise for what Greenberg ultimately offers.
